** How to Buy a $20m Business as a First-Timer

------------------------------------------------------------

When Alan Turkus found a business with a mission, he knew he'd found the right fit for the final chapter of his career.

How to Build a Franchise Holdco

https://acquiringminds.co/webinars/anatomy-of-a-franchise-holdco

Franchises and ETA play so well together.

In this webinar, Connor Groce covers:

* Single-brand roll-ups vs. multi-brand portfolios

* Franchise acquisitions: sourcing, diligence, and integration

* Institutional capital in franchising

* Industries with the most opportunity in franchising

* Case studies

Connor Groce has owned or operated franchise units in multiple systems.

He has grown his own portfolio through multiple successful acquisitions and learned the power that acquisitions can play in long-term value creation.

Watch this recorded webinar to learn from an expert at the intersection of ETA and franchising.

Watch Recording (free) (https://acquiringminds.co/webinars/anatomy-of-a-franchise-holdco)

It's hard to re-enter the corporate world after being out of it for seven years.

Especially if you're in your 50s.

‍This was the situation that today's guest Alan Turkus found himself in.

But what that uncomfortable phase prompted Alan to do was revisit an idea he'd had in the back of his mind from his business school days: buy an existing business.

Now that prospect wasn't just a workaround to find a job.

It was about the fact that Alan's level of experience — having run business units at Amazon, P&L experience — meant he sought meaty management responsibility.

‍Owning your own business, especially one that does $20m and employs 150 people, is certainly that.

We discuss in detail the financials for how he was able to acquire such a large business. (Yes, he had investors; we learn who they are.)

We discuss doing this with an SBA loan.

‍We explore Alan's attempt to use ROBS, and why it wouldn't work.

This is a franchise business, so we learn Alan's thoughts there. (Hint: like many of you probably, he never thought he'd be a franchisee.)

And finally, we discuss purpose.

‍Alan's search ended not when the quantitative considerations lined up, but when the qualitative stuff did. There is mission to the home healthcare and hospice business that Alan bought, and it was exactly that that had been missing from the other deals he looked at.

** Key Takeaways

------------------------------------------------------------

1. Alan Turkus, a 57-year-old executive with Amazon P&L experience, faced challenges re-entering the corporate workforce after 7 years out, prompting him to pursue buying an existing business rather than seeking traditional employment, which he viewed as less secure.

2. His search focused on larger businesses in Minneapolis-Saint Paul with at least $1 million in EBITDA, ultimately leading to the acquisition of Interim Healthcare of the Twin Cities, a home health and hospice business that strongly resonated with his desire for mission-driven work.

3. The business generates approximately $20 million in annual revenue with $2 million in EBITDA and employs 150 people, representing a substantial recovery from COVID-related challenges that had previously impacted facilities-based healthcare services.

4. Alan structured the acquisition at roughly 4x EBITDA for $8 million total, including $4 million from an SBA loan, $1.9 million in equity ($400k personal, $1.5M from investors), and two $1.5 million seller notes tied to performance metrics over the first and second 12-month periods post-closing.

5. Despite owning slightly more than 50% of the business and receiving a $150,000 base salary, Alan partnered with experienced ETA investors Grant Hensel, Jacob Hall, and Adam Markley, viewing the reduced ownership as worthwhile for accessing a larger, more stable business with strong management infrastructure and mission alignment.

------------------------------------------------------------
